9:2.text: As he spake by the mouth of his holy prophets, which have been since the world began:

provenance.other: “by the mouth of his holy prophets” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 1:70. The one near neighbour is Acts 3:21, which reads “by the mouth of all his holy prophets”; Jacob has no “all”.
provenance.alternative: Acts 3:21, on the subject matter rather than the wording.
provenance.significance: The two verses divide the sentence between them. Jacob's wording is Zacharias's — the seven-word run without Peter's “all” — while Jacob's subject is Peter's: the restoration of Israel to its own. Acts 3:21 is “the times of restitution of all things, which God hath spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets”, and Jacob's clause runs on to “until the time cometh that they shall be restored”. Recovering the Acts context also recovers what stands two verses later at Acts 3:22-23, the Deuteronomy 18 prophet-like-Moses oracle that 1 Nephi 22:20 takes in its Acts form. The seam between the two verses is where the interest is: the phrasing of the one, the argument of the other.

9:2.note: Jacob's summary of prophetic testimony — “he hath spoken unto the Jews, by the mouth of his holy prophets, even from the beginning down” — reproduces seven consecutive words of Luke 1:70 exactly. This is well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold for a quotation and is catalogued as an allusion, but the run is verbatim and the phrase is a KJV singleton, and the Benedictus is the KJV's one place where prophetic speech, the covenant with the fathers and Israel's deliverance stand in a single sentence — which is precisely the three-part subject of 2 Nephi 9:1-2. Note also the tail: Luke has “which have been since the world began”, Acts 3:21 “since the world began”, and Jacob “even from the beginning down, from generation to generation”, which paraphrases the same idea in the KJV's own register without taking either wording.

9:4.text: And though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God:

provenance.other: “in my flesh shall I see God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Job 19:26.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the borrowing acquires its argument. Job 19:25-26 is the KJV's locus classicus for bodily resurrection — “I know that my redeemer liveth … yet in my flesh shall I see God” — and it is spoken by a man insisting on vindication against friends who have told him he is wrong. Jacob is two days into a temple sermon to a divided people and is about to spend fifty verses on the resurrection of the body; he opens the argument by putting Job's certainty into the first person plural. The turn from Job's “my flesh” to “our bodies” is the whole rhetorical move: the one man's private hope of seeing God in his own flesh becomes a congregation's.

9:4.note: “Our flesh must waste away and die; nevertheless, in our bodies, we shall see God.” Both halves of Job 19:26 are here in order — the body destroyed, and then God seen in the body — and the second half is a KJV singleton. Jacob's substitution of “bodies” for “flesh” is not a weakening of the link but a consequence of his own first clause, which has already spent “flesh” on the corpse (“our flesh must waste away”); having used the KJV's word for what dies, he needs another for what sees. The 1830 reads “thou hast searched much” at the head of the verse, second person singular against the plural “many of you” that follows, and 1920 regularised it to “ye”; the 1830's awkwardness is the older reading.

9:6.text: Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned:

provenance.other: “death passed upon all men” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 5:12.
provenance.significance: Metalepsis of the plainest kind. Romans 5:12 is a protasis with no apodosis — Paul's “as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men” breaks off and is not completed until 5:18-19, and the completion is that by one man's righteousness the free gift came upon all men. Jacob borrows the broken protasis and supplies his own apodosis on the spot: “as death hath passed upon all men … there must needs be a power of resurrection.” The suspended sentence in Romans is finished in 2 Nephi, and finished with the Adam-Christ symmetry that Paul finishes it with. Whatever else it is, this is a reader of Romans 5 who knows where the sentence is going.

9:6.note: Five words verbatim, and the one KJV verse they come from. Jacob's clause reads “For as death hath passed upon all men, to fulfil the merciful plan of the Great Creator, there must needs be a power of resurrection” — Paul's “so” becomes “as”, which converts a conclusion into a premise, and the rest of the verse then argues from the fall to the resurrection exactly as Romans 5:12-21 does. The run is far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and this is not one of his passages; it is catalogued as a quotation on the strength of the singleton rather than the length, per CONVENTIONS §2. The chapter's whole atonement argument is built on the Pauline pair Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15, and this is where the first of them enters.

9:7.text: For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.

provenance.other: “corruptible must put on incorruption” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 15:53; “put on incorruption” occurs in exactly two, 15:53 and 15:54.
provenance.significance: 1 Corinthians 15:53-54 is the verse on which Paul's resurrection chapter turns from argument to triumph — the putting on of incorruption is what makes “Death is swallowed up in victory” sayable. Jacob takes the clause and negates it: “save it should be an infinite atonement, this corruption could not put on incorruption.” The borrowed words are used to state the condition under which Paul's sentence would have been false. Recovering the context recovers what 15:54 goes on to promise, and Jacob's next three verses (8-13) are that promise: the flesh rises, hell delivers up its captives, all men become incorruptible and immortal.

9:7.note: The one substitution carries the argument. Paul writes “this corruptible must put on incorruption”, an adjective naming the perishable body; the 1830 reads “this corruption could not put on incorruption”, an abstract noun naming the state, which is what lets the sentence be about the atonement rather than about a body. The 1830 already has “corruption” — this is not a later editorial drift — and “incorruptible, and immortal” returns at 9:13 to complete the pair 1 Corinthians 15:53 makes (incorruption and immortality). Note that Romans 5:12 entered one verse earlier at 9:6: the two Pauline resurrection chapters arrive together and in the order in which a reader working from a Bible would meet them.

9:8.text: O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!

provenance.other: “O the depth” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, of which only Romans 11:33 is an exclamation of this shape; the other two (Psalm 107:26, Micah 7:19) use “the depths” of literal water.
provenance.significance: Romans 11:33 is where Paul breaks off an argument about Israel's rejection and restoration to exclaim at the wisdom of God, and 2 Nephi 9 is an argument about Israel's restoration (9:1-2) punctuated by exactly such exclamations — six of them, at 9:8, 9:10, 9:13, 9:17, 9:19 and 9:20. The doxology is not decoration in either place: it is what an argument about covenant reversal does when it reaches a point it cannot argue past.

9:8.note: “O the wisdom of God! his mercy and grace!” The KJV has one exclamation of this construction — vocative O, an abstract attribute, of God — and it is Romans 11:33's “O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” Jacob's is not a verbal reproduction; the shared material is the syntax and the pairing of God's wisdom with his mercy, which Romans 11:30-32 has just spent three verses on (“that he might have mercy upon all”). The link is recorded at the first of the six exclamations and the rest are listed as recurrences rather than given rows of their own.
9:8.whyNot: No content word is shared beyond “God” and “wisdom”, both far too common to point anywhere. The form could as easily be Jacob's own, and the exclamatory O is available from the Psalms in bulk. This is graded moderate as a formal echo, and a reader who declines it loses nothing else in the chapter.

9:9.text: And no marvel; for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light.

provenance.other: “an angel of light” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 11:14.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is about false apostles: the transformation into an angel of light is offered as the reason “his ministers also be transformed as the ministers of righteousness” (11:15). Jacob is warning a congregation against a being who “stirreth up the children of men unto secret combinations of murder”, and he reaches for the KJV's one verse about Satan disguised as a messenger of God. The suppressed half of the source is the half about the disguised ministers, which is the danger a sermon delivered from a temple would have most reason to name and does not.

9:9.note: “Who transformeth himself nigh unto an angel of light.” The phrase is a KJV singleton and the subject is the same being. Two departures are worth recording. Paul's verb is passive — “Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light” — where Jacob's is active and reflexive, which makes the disguise a thing the devil does rather than a thing done to him; and Jacob's “nigh unto” is a hedge with no counterpart in the KJV, conceding that the resemblance is not complete. Both changes push in the same direction, toward an agent who counterfeits and does not quite succeed.

9:9.text: Ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do. He was a murderer from the beginning, and abode not in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it.

provenance.other: “father of it”, the KJV's phrase for the devil as author of lying, occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 8:44.
provenance.significance: John 8:44 holds in one sentence the two things Jacob's verse holds: “He was a murderer from the beginning … he is a liar, and the father of it.” Jacob's clause runs “to remain with the father of lies, in misery … and stirreth up the children of men unto secret combinations of murder”, and the pairing of the lie with the murder is not a general association — it is John's, in John's order, from the verse where Jesus tells his hearers whose children they are. The metalepsis is in the address: John 8:44 is spoken to covenant Israelites who have claimed Abraham as their father, which is exactly Jacob's audience.

9:9.note: The KJV has no phrase “father of lies”; it has John 8:44's “he is a liar, and the father of it”, which the Book of Mormon compresses into the noun phrase later English would settle on. Two independent contacts sit in one verse of John and one verse of Jacob — the lie and its fatherhood, and the murder from the beginning — and the same chapter of John returns at 2 Nephi 9:38 (“wo unto all they that die in their sins”, John 8:21, 24). A chapter that touches John 8 twice, thirty verses apart, at its two most distinctive phrases, is reading John 8.

9:12.text: And the sea gave up the dead which were in it; and death and hell delivered up the dead which were in them: and they were judged every man according to their works.

provenance.other: “death and hell delivered up the dead” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 20:13.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's structural borrowing and it explains a puzzle. Revelation 20:13-14 runs: death and hell deliver up their dead, they are judged, and then “death and hell were cast into the lake of fire”. 2 Nephi 9 does the same three things in the same order — death and hell deliver up their dead here at 9:12, the judgment follows at 9:15, and the lake of fire and brimstone arrives at 9:16 and again at 9:19 and 9:26. So the “awful monster, death and hell” that Jacob names at 9:10 and cannot stop naming is not a free-standing image: it is John's paired personification, borrowed with the plot it belongs to. Recovering Revelation 20 recovers the reason the lake of fire has to come three verses later.

9:12.note: Jacob's “death and hell must deliver up its dead” reproduces the KJV's clause with one change of number, and the surrounding sentences unpack it: “hell must deliver up its captive spirits, and the grave must deliver up its captive bodies”. The 1830's singular “its dead” against a plural subject was corrected to “their” in 1920 — the sort of grammatical roughness the first edition preserves and later editions smooth, and here the direction of the change is away from the source, since the KJV reads “the dead which were in them”. The link is placed at 9:12, where the wording is, rather than at 9:10 where the monster is first named.

9:13.text: He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches; To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the midst of the paradise of God.

provenance.other: “paradise of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 2:7.
provenance.significance: In Revelation 2:7 the paradise of God is where the tree of life stands and is promised to him that overcometh; in 2 Nephi 9:13 it is a holding place that “must deliver up the spirits of the righteous” at the resurrection. The borrowing has moved the phrase from a destination to a waiting room, and the sense it takes is Luke 23:43's rather than John's — the paradise a dying man enters today. The two-word phrase carries the geography of one text and the doctrine of another.

9:13.note: The disembodied-spirits paradise of 2 Nephi 9:13 is named with the KJV's one occurrence of “paradise of God”, from the letter to Ephesus. This is graded moderate because two words, however rare their combination, are thin evidence, and because the chapter has already shown it will take an eschatological furnishing from Revelation and use it structurally (Revelation 20:13 one verse earlier). That prior borrowing is the reason to take this one seriously: the paradise arrives in a sentence built out of the same book's twentieth chapter.
9:13.whyNot: Two words. “Paradise” alone appears in three KJV verses and any of them would license the idea; only the genitive construction is distinctive, and a writer with Luke 23:43 in mind could arrive at “paradise of God” without Revelation.

9:13.text: And so it is written, The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit.

provenance.route: Genesis 2:7 → 1 Corinthians 15:45 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “living soul” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Genesis 2:7, 1 Corinthians 15:45 and Revelation 16:3. tools/mediation-check.py finds no decisive divergence between Genesis 2:7 and 1 Corinthians 15:45 at any point 2 Nephi 9:13 reproduces, so the mediation is argued from context rather than from wording.
provenance.significance: The phrase has been inverted in transit. For Paul, “the first man Adam was made a living soul” is the *low* term of the contrast: the living soul is the natural body that dies, set against “the last Adam … a quickening spirit”. Jacob applies it to the resurrected — “all men become incorruptible, and immortal, and they are living souls” — which is Paul's own vocabulary used for Paul's opposite. That is not a misreading so much as a collapse of the antithesis, and it is the kind of thing that shows a source being used rather than merely shared.

9:13.note: The mediation is the finding here, and the tool cannot settle it: Genesis 2:7 and 1 Corinthians 15:45 do not differ at “living soul”, so the wording is neutral between them. The context is not. The sentence around the phrase is 1 Corinthians 15's and nowhere else's — “incorruptible, and immortal” is 15:53's pair, the resurrection body is 15's subject, and 15:53 has already been used at 2 Nephi 9:7 six verses earlier. Genesis 2:7 supplies the phrase to Paul; Paul supplies it to Jacob. Recorded as OT-via-NT on that argument, and a reader who prefers direct-OT is disagreeing with an inference, not with a word count.

9:14.text: I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels.

provenance.other: “robe of righteousness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 61:10.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 61:10 is a garment verse in a chapter about reversal — the garments of salvation and the robe of righteousness are given to those who had ashes and mourning. Jacob has just built the same reversal out of clothing: the wicked receive “a perfect knowledge of all our guilt, and our uncleanness, and our nakedness”, and the righteous “their enjoyment, and their righteousness, being clothed with purity”. The nakedness the borrowing implies is Isaiah's unspoken opposite, and the resurrection-judgment scene in which Jacob sets it makes the clothing an eschatological verdict rather than a festal ornament.

9:14.note: A KJV singleton, taken with its verb of clothing intact and set against a nakedness the source does not mention. This is the machine stream's one solid proposal in the chapter's first half (it scored Isaiah 61:10 at 9:14 on a five-word run), and it is right: nothing else in the KJV pairs a robe with righteousness. Note that Jacob does not take Isaiah's other garment, the “garments of salvation” of the same verse — a selective borrower, not a copyist.

9:15.text: For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad.

provenance.other: “appear before the judgment seat” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 5:10; “judgment seat” alone occurs in eleven, most of them Roman magistrates in Acts. Romans 14:10, the near neighbour, reads “stand before the judgment seat”.
provenance.significance: Paul's judgment seat is Christ's, and the clause that follows it — “that every one may receive the things done in his body” — is a judgment on embodied deeds. Jacob has spent nine verses arguing that the body must be restored to the spirit before judgment can occur, and he reaches the judgment seat only once every man has been made immortal: “when all men shall have passed from this first death unto life, insomuch as they have become immortal, they must appear before the judgment seat.” The borrowed phrase arrives with Paul's reason for it already supplied by the argument.

9:15.note: The verb decides between the two Pauline judgment-seat verses. Romans 14:10 has men *stand* before it, 2 Corinthians 5:10 has them *appear* before it, and Jacob's “must appear before the judgment seat” takes the second — and takes “must all” with it (“all men … they must appear”). The 1830 prints “judgment seat” as two words and 1920 hyphenates it to “judgment-seat”, which is a small piece of evidence for the direction of transmission: the first edition has the KJV's typography, and the later edition has the nineteenth-century compound.

9:16.text: He that is unjust, let him be unjust still: and he which is filthy, let him be filthy still: and he that is righteous, let him be righteous still: and he that is holy, let him be holy still.

provenance.other: “filthy still” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 22:11, which also supplies “righteous still”.
provenance.significance: Revelation 22:11 stands eleven verses from the end of the Bible and is the sealing-up of moral destiny: after it there is nothing but the invitation and the curse on adders. Jacob quotes it as the ground of an appeal to men who can still change — “that they which are righteous, shall be righteous still, and they which are filthy, shall be filthy still” — and then spends thirty-five verses urging repentance. The borrowed verse says the door is shut; the sermon it is quoted in is the door being held open, and the tension is not resolved.

9:16.note: Both halves of Revelation 22:11's second pair, in the KJV's own words and in the KJV's own antithetical construction, introduced by “it is his eternal word, which cannot pass away”. The KJV has jussives (“let him be righteous still”) and Jacob has futures (“shall be righteous still”), which converts John's permission into a prediction — the difference between a decree ratifying what men have become and a law about what they will be. The 1830's “they which are righteous” was modernised to “those who” in 1920; the first edition keeps the KJV's relative pronoun and shows the borrowing more plainly.

9:16.text: Then shall he say also unto them on the left hand, Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels:

provenance.other: “the devil and his angels” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:41.
provenance.significance: The finding is the division of labour with 9:18. Matthew 25:31-46 is one judgment scene with two halves, a curse on the left hand (25:41, “Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels”) and a blessing on the right (25:34, “inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world”). Jacob takes the curse here and the blessing two verses later, keeps the shared word “prepared” in both, and reverses Matthew's order so that his own sermon ends on the blessing. The sheep-and-goats scene has been dismantled and reassembled around Jacob's antithesis, and neither half is quoted without the other.

9:16.note: Two runs from Matthew 25:41 — “the devil and his angels” and “into everlasting fire, prepared for” — and a third from 25:46, “shall go away into everlasting”, whose noun Jacob replaces (Matthew's “everlasting punishment” for Matthew's own “everlasting fire”). The changed word in 25:41 is the beneficiary: Matthew's fire is prepared *for the devil and his angels*, and Jacob's is prepared “for them”, the filthy, having identified them with the devil and his angels in the preceding clause. That identification is Jacob's contribution and it is what lets one verse of Matthew do the work of two.

9:16.text: And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name.

provenance.route: Revelation 14:10-11 and 20:10 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “ascendeth up for ever and ever” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 14:11. Revelation 14:10 supplies “tormented with fire and brimstone”; Revelation 20:10 supplies “the lake of fire and brimstone”.
provenance.significance: Jacob's sentence — “their torment is a lake of fire and brimstone, whose flames ascendeth up forever and ever” — fuses two verses that the KJV keeps six chapters apart, and takes from each what the other lacks. Revelation 14:10-11 has the torment and the ascending, but its column is smoke and its fire is not a lake; Revelation 20:10 has the lake of fire and brimstone, but nothing ascends from it. What ascends in the Book of Mormon is flames, which is in neither. The composite is the evidence: a writer working from one verse does not produce a phrase that requires two.

9:16.note: The 1830 reads “whose flames ascendeth up forever and ever”, with a plural subject and a singular verb that 1920 tidied to “flame”. The verb is the borrowed word — the KJV's one “ascendeth up for ever and ever” has smoke for its subject, and substituting flames for smoke is what forced the grammatical roughness the first edition preserves and the later edition removed. This is 1830 evidence of the useful kind: the awkwardness is a fingerprint of the substitution.

9:18.text: Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God.

provenance.other: “despising the shame” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 12:2.
provenance.significance: In Hebrews the one who endures the cross and despises the shame is Jesus, and the saints are told to look at him; in 2 Nephi it is the saints themselves who “have endured the crosses of the world, and despised the shame of it”. The transfer is the point, and it is the transfer Hebrews 12:1-3 is arguing for — the cloud of witnesses, the race set before us, the author and finisher of faith held up as the pattern. Jacob has taken the conclusion Hebrews draws and stated it as though it were the premise.

9:18.note: Two clauses of Hebrews 12:2 in Hebrews' order — the cross endured, the shame despised — with each term pluralised or possessed: “the crosses of the world”, “the shame of it”. The pluralised cross is the departure that matters, since it converts a single historical execution into a class of hardships, which is precisely what a sermon exhorting a congregation needs it to be. Jacob is not quoting a christological verse about Christ; he is quoting it about his hearers, and the KJV singleton is what shows the verse is in view at all.

9:18.text: Then shall the King say unto them on his right hand, Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world:

provenance.other: “prepared for you from the foundation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:34; “from the foundation of the world” alone occurs in six.
provenance.significance: See the note at 9:16. The two halves of Matthew's judgment scene are distributed across Jacob's antithesis: the fire prepared for the devil and his angels at 9:16, the kingdom prepared from the foundation of the world at 9:18, with “prepared” standing in both as it does in Matthew. What Jacob adds is the reason the righteous inherit — “they which have endured the crosses of the world” — which Matthew gives as feeding the hungry and visiting the prisoner. The frame is Matthew's and the criterion is not.

9:18.note: Seven words of Matthew 25:34 with one pronoun changed: “inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” becomes “they shall inherit the Kingdom of God, which was prepared for them from the foundation of the world”. The shift from second to third person follows from Jacob's syntax — Matthew's King is addressing the blessed, Jacob is describing them — and the inserted “of God” is his, since Matthew's King says only “the kingdom”. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his passages, catalogued as a quotation on the singleton and the verbatim run.

9:23.text: Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.

provenance.other: “be baptized every one of you in the name” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 2:38. Frederick observes that the exact phrase “baptized in his name”, which is Jacob's form here and at 9:24, is unique to Mormon scripture and is not found in the Bible — a real qualification to any claim of verbal dependence, and one that should be recorded against this row rather than argued away.
provenance.significance: Acts 2:38 is Peter's answer to “what shall we do?” on the day of Pentecost, and it is the KJV's one place where repentance and baptism are commanded together in a single imperative to a crowd. Jacob's “he commandeth all men that they must repent, and be baptised in his name” is that imperative turned into a report of a standing commandment. Recovering the context recovers what makes the borrowing anachronistic in an interesting rather than a trivial way: the model is not a prophecy of baptism but the first Christian administration of it.

9:23.note: The wording is Peter's minus the possessive: Acts 2:38 has “in the name of Jesus Christ” where Jacob has “in his name”, the referent having been supplied by the preceding verses. That difference is not incidental, and Frederick makes something of it — his discussion of 2 Nephi 9:23-24 notes that “baptized in his name” as such occurs nowhere in the Bible and is a phrase peculiar to Mormon scripture. So the case here rests on the pairing (repent + be baptized + a name) rather than on a reproduced string, which is why this is graded high rather than certain. The chapter's own next verse extends the list, and the John 1:12 row at 9:24 is where Frederick's argument properly sits.

9:24.text: But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name:

provenance.other: The shared material is “believe … on/in his name”. Frederick treats the phrase at 2 Nephi 9:24 as an allusion to John 1:12, notes that the pairing of “repent” with “believe in his name” occurs seven times in Mormon scripture and nowhere in the Bible, and concludes that the allusion serves a rhetorical rather than an interpretive function — echoing an authoritative text for a nineteenth-century audience rather than engaging John's argument.
provenance.significance: The interest is in what the borrowing does to the source. In John 1:12 belief on his name is sufficient and binary — those who receive him are given power to become the sons of God, and that is the whole condition. In 2 Nephi 9:24 believing in his name is one item in a list of four (repent, believe, be baptised, endure to the end), any of which can be failed. Frederick's reading is that Jacob expands John's condition into a set of requirements and thereby loses John's polarity; on that reading the echo is doing rhetorical rather than exegetical work, which is a claim about the whole Book of Mormon's use of John and not only about this verse.

9:24.note: This is the one row in the chapter where a scholar we hold has actually treated the passage. Frederick's chapter on the Book of Mormon's Johannine language discusses 2 Nephi 9:23-24 at length, identifies “believe in his name” as reaching back to John 1:11-12, and argues that its function is rhetorical. The catalogue records the link on his evidence and grades it moderate on ours: the shared words are four common ones in a common order, and the case rests on the Johannine formula rather than on rarity. Note that his conclusion is a deflationary one — he finds no attempt to engage John beyond the repetition of its language — so citing him here is citing an argument about the *kind* of borrowing, not a claim that John 1:12 is the only possible source.
bibliography: Frederick 2016: ch. 4, on 2 Nephi 9:23-24 and John 1:11-12

9:24.text: He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved; but he that believeth not shall be damned.

provenance.route: Mark 16:16 and Matthew 10:22 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “shall be damned” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 16:16; “endureth to the end” occurs in exactly one, Matthew 10:22.
provenance.significance: Mark 16:16 is the KJV's one sentence holding belief, baptism, salvation and damnation together, and it is a conditional with two arms. Jacob keeps both terms and collapses the arms into one: “if they will not repent and believe in his name, and be baptised in his name, and endure to the end, they must be damned.” Matthew 10:22's endurance clause is spliced in from a persecution discourse where enduring to the end is surviving betrayal by one's family — which is a harder thing than the list Jacob has made it the last item of, and the harder sense is the one his sermon has been arguing for since 9:18's crosses of the world.

9:24.note: Two KJV singletons in one sentence, from two Gospels, in the order Mark gives them: believe, be baptised, and then the damnation that is Mark's alternative. Jacob's verb is “must be damned”, a necessity, against Mark's simple future — consistent with the chapter's argument that the law's demands are met or not met and that justice, not caprice, decides. The single word “damned” is what makes the verse identifiable at all; “believe” and “baptised” between them fill hundreds of KJV verses, and the row would not stand on them.

9:25.text: Because the law worketh wrath: for where no law is, there is no transgression.

provenance.route: Romans 4:15 and 5:13 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “where no law is” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 4:15. Romans 5:13 states the same principle in different words: “sin is not imputed when there is no law”.
provenance.significance: Both Pauline verses stand inside the argument 2 Nephi 9 has been running since 9:6, and 5:13 is four verses past the “death passed upon all men” that Jacob quoted there. Paul uses the no-law principle to explain how death reigned from Adam to Moses; Jacob uses it to exempt those who never received the law from the demands of justice. The premise is Paul's and the conclusion is not — Romans is explaining a fact about history, 2 Nephi is granting a class of persons a claim on mercy.

9:25.note: “Where there is no law given, there is no punishment; and where there is no punishment, there is no condemnation.” The construction is Romans 4:15's — a conditional of the form *where no X, no Y*, which the KJV uses of law in that one verse — and Jacob extends it into a chain of three, each link taking the previous consequent as its antecedent. The chain is a piece of scholastic reasoning built on a Pauline formula, and the word Jacob adds at the head is “given”, which does the exempting: it is not that no law exists but that none was given to them. Graded moderate because no distinctive string is reproduced; what is borrowed is a sentence shape and a doctrine.
9:25.whyNot: The wording is not reproduced. Paul's terms are law and transgression; Jacob's are law, punishment and condemnation, and only “law” is shared. A reader could hold that this is common eighteenth-century covenant theology reaching Jacob by way of the pulpit rather than by way of Romans 4.

9:26.text: Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it.

provenance.other: “unto God who gave it” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ecclesiastes 12:7.
provenance.significance: Ecclesiastes 12:7 is a death verse — “then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it” — and the return is a dissolution, the undoing of Genesis 2:7 in Genesis 2:7's own vocabulary. Jacob turns the same clause into a verse about deliverance: those without the law “are restored to that God who gave them breath”. Restored, not returned; and the breath rather than the spirit, which pulls Genesis 2:7's “breathed into his nostrils the breath of life” back into a sentence Ecclesiastes had built out of it.

9:26.note: The distinctive material is the relative clause: God characterised as the one who gave what is now being given back. The KJV does this once. Jacob's two changes both raise the temperature — “restored” for “return”, which makes the movement a gift rather than a forfeiture, and “breath” for “it”, which names what Ecclesiastes leaves as a pronoun and names it with Genesis 2:7's word. Graded moderate: the clause is short, and a writer could reach it independently from Genesis, though not with the KJV's exact relative construction.

9:28.text: For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness.

provenance.other: “the wisdom of this world” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, 1 Corinthians 1:20, 2:6 and 3:19 — every one of them in the same letter and the same argument.
provenance.significance: 1 Corinthians 1-3 is a sustained attack on human wisdom as a qualification for the gospel, and 2 Nephi 9:28-29, 42-43 is the same attack with the same moves in the same order: the learned think they are wise (1 Cor 1:20, 3:18), their wisdom is foolishness with God (3:19), and the remedy is to become a fool in order to be wise (3:18). Recovering the Corinthian context recovers a qualification Jacob then supplies himself at 9:29 — “to be learned is good, if it so be that they hearken unto the counsels of God” — which is a concession Paul does not make in those chapters and which reads like a reader correcting the source's excess.

9:28.note: “When they are learned, they think they are wise … Wherefore, their wisdom is foolishness, and it profiteth them not.” The predicate is Paul's, from the one KJV verse that says the wisdom of this world is foolishness, and the reasoning around it is Paul's too: those who suppose they know of themselves, set against the counsel of God. The chapter returns to the same three chapters of 1 Corinthians twice more, at 9:42 (become a fool, puffed up) and by implication at 9:43, which is the signal that this is a source being worked rather than a proverb in the air. Note that Jacob has stated as a conclusion (“their wisdom is foolishness”) what Paul states as a fact about God's estimate (“foolishness with God”), dropping the qualifier that made Paul's claim bearable.

9:30.text: But ye have despised the poor. Do not rich men oppress you, and draw you before the judgment seats?

provenance.route: James 2:5-6 and 5:1, with Luke 6:24 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “despised the poor” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 2:6; “woe unto you that are rich” occurs in exactly one, Luke 6:24; “ye rich men” occurs in exactly one, James 5:1.
provenance.significance: Jacob's woe to the rich reproduces the three elements the New Testament keeps in three different places: the woe itself (Luke 6:24), the despising of the poor (James 2:6), and the perishing of the treasure (James 5:1-3, where the rich men's gold is cankered). James 2:6 is the sharpest of them because its next clause is “do not rich men oppress you, and draw you before the judgment seats?” — and Jacob's chapter has stood the rich before a judgment seat fifteen verses earlier at 9:15. The suppressed half of the source is the courtroom, which the sermon has already supplied.

9:30.note: Three KJV singletons converge on one sentence: “wo unto the rich, which are rich as to the things of the world. For because that they are rich, they despise the poor, and they persecute the meek.” The woe-formula is Luke's, the despising of the poor is James's, and the persecution is James 2:6's oppression. Jacob's added qualification — rich “as to the things of the world” — is the same move he makes at 9:29 about learning: the condemnation is narrowed to a disposition, not the condition. James 2:5, “hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith”, supplies the terms of that narrowing.

9:30.text: For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.

provenance.other: “where your treasure is” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 6:21 and Luke 12:34, which are verbally identical; the wording cannot decide between them.
provenance.significance: Matthew 6:21 sits between the treasures laid up in heaven and the impossibility of serving God and mammon, and Jacob's sentence draws the conclusion Matthew leaves implicit: “their hearts are upon their treasures; wherefore their treasure is their God.” The heart following the treasure becomes the treasure being the God, which is Matthew 6:24 four verses on. The borrowing has read to the end of the paragraph.

9:30.note: Matthew's aphorism is inverted rather than quoted — the KJV moves from treasure to heart, and Jacob from heart to treasure — but the pairing is Matthew's and it arrives with Matthew 6:24's conclusion attached. The choice of Matthew over the identical Luke 12:34 cannot be made on wording; it is made on the chapter's own habits, since 2 Nephi 9:41-42 goes on to use Matthew 7:14 and Matthew 7:8, from the same sermon and a page later in the same Gospel. That is an argument from company, not from words, and it is offered as such.

9:30.text: But Peter said unto him, Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money.

provenance.other: “money perish with thee” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 8:20.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's most interesting suppressed context if it holds. Acts 8:20 is Peter to Simon Magus — “thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money” — the KJV's one rebuke to a man who tried to buy what is not for sale. Twenty verses later Jacob closes his sermon with Isaiah 55:1-2, the KJV's one invitation to buy without money: “he that hath no money, come buy and eat.” A chapter that condemns the rich with the words spoken over Simon's silver and then offers wine and milk without price has arranged its own two ends around the same question, and neither Isaiah nor Acts says so.

9:30.note: “Their treasure shall perish with them also.” The construction is Acts 8:20's — a possession commanded to perish along with its owner — and the KJV says this once. The link is graded moderate and typed as an echo because Jacob's noun is “treasure” where Peter's is “money”, and because the sentence would be intelligible without the source; what recommends it is the shape (perish *with them*, not merely perish) and the chapter's return to money at 9:50-51.
9:30.whyNot: Only three words are shared and one of them is a preposition. “Perish” is common in the KJV and Jacob has used it three times in this passage already (9:28, 9:31, 9:32), so the verb may simply be his. A reader who declines this row loses the Simon Magus reading and nothing else.

9:33.text: Egypt, and Judah, and Edom, and the children of Ammon, and Moab, and all that are in the utmost corners, that dwell in the wilderness: for all these nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in the heart.

provenance.route: Jeremiah 9:26 / Ezekiel 44:7 / Acts 7:51 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “uncircumcised in heart” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Ezekiel 44:7, Ezekiel 44:9 and Acts 7:51; Jeremiah 9:26 has “uncircumcised in the heart”. The Book of Mormon reads “uncircumcised of heart”, which matches none of them exactly. tools/mediation-check.py finds no decisive divergence between Ezekiel 44:7 and Acts 7:51 at any point 2 Nephi 9:33 reproduces, so the mediation is recorded as uncertain rather than guessed.
provenance.significance: Each candidate brings a different audience. Jeremiah 9:26 is the one that says “all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in the heart”, which is Jacob's congregation exactly; Ezekiel 44:7 uses the phrase to bar strangers from the sanctuary, which is the wrong audience for a temple sermon addressed to the covenant people themselves; Acts 7:51 is Stephen before the council, an indictment delivered by a man about to be killed for delivering it, which is the closest in rhetorical situation to a preacher who ends by shaking his garments and declaring himself rid of his hearers' blood (9:44). The phrase is one of the few in the KJV whose every occurrence is an accusation from inside the covenant.

9:33.note: “Wo unto the uncircumcised of heart: for a knowledge of their iniquities shall smite them at the last day.” The preposition is the problem and the reason this is graded moderate: the KJV never says “of heart”, and the three verses that say “in heart” or “in the heart” do not differ from one another at any word Jacob reproduces, so nothing in the wording can adjudicate between them. Jeremiah 9:26 is listed as the source because it alone applies the charge to the whole house of Israel, which is what Jacob is doing; Acts 7:51 and Ezekiel 44:7 are recorded as composites, and a reader who prefers either is not contradicted by any evidence this catalogue can produce.
9:33.whyNot: No exact string is shared. The idea of an uncircumcised heart is available from Deuteronomy 10:16 and 30:6 as well, in different words, and “uncircumcised” is common enough in the KJV that the collocation with heart is the only distinctive thing here.

9:34.text: And thou, Capernaum, which art exalted to heaven, shalt be thrust down to hell.

provenance.other: “thrust down to hell” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 10:15. The Matthean parallel at 11:23 reads “brought down to hell”, so the verb decides the source.
provenance.significance: Luke 10:15 is the woe on Capernaum: “thou, Capernaum, which art exalted to heaven, shalt be thrust down to hell.” It belongs to a series of woes on cities, which is the form Jacob is in the middle of — ten woes running from 9:27 to 9:38. And the same chapter of Luke returns at 9:43, where the things hidden from the wise and prudent are Luke 10:21's. Two of the chapter's borrowings come from a single page of Luke, and both come from the sayings the woes are made of.

9:34.note: A KJV singleton, taken with its verb intact, and the machine stream's best find in this chapter — the n-gram run flagged it at both 9:34 and 9:36. Matthew's parallel says “brought down to hell” and Jacob says “thrust down to hell”, so this is one of the cases where a single word settles which Gospel is in view, in the manner of the mediation tests at 1 Nephi 22:20. The phrase is used twice within four verses (of the liar at 9:34 and of the whoremonger at 9:36); the second is Jacob using his own formula and is registered as a recurrence rather than a second borrowing.

9:38.text: Then said Jesus again unto them, I go my way, and ye shall seek me, and shall die in your sins: whither I go, ye cannot come.

provenance.other: “die in your sins” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 8:21 and John 8:24, and John 8:24 has it twice.
provenance.significance: The metalepsis inverts the source. John 8:21 runs: “ye shall die in your sins: whither I go, ye cannot come” — dying in one's sins means being unable to come where Christ is. Jacob's version is the opposite: “they shall return to God, and behold his face, and remain in their sins.” They do come; they see him; and the sins are still there. The horror is relocated from exclusion to presence, which is exactly the doctrine the chapter has been building since 9:15, where every man without exception must appear before the judgment seat. Recovering John 8 shows what Jacob had to change to make his own eschatology work.

9:38.note: The last and heaviest of the ten woes takes its wording from John 8, whose 44th verse supplied the father of lies at 9:9 — the chapter's two Johannine borrowings sit twenty-nine verses apart and both come from the same discourse. Jacob's “die in their sins” is the third person of John's second person, addressed to a congregation rather than to opponents. The phrase is a near-singleton confined to one chapter of one Gospel, which is what makes the identification safe; “sins” and “die” separately would prove nothing.

9:39.text: For to be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life and peace.

provenance.other: “carnally minded” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 8:6. “life eternal” occurs in exactly four, of which Matthew 25:46 is the one this chapter has already used, at 9:16.
provenance.significance: Romans 8:6's second half is “life and peace”, and peace is what Jacob drops. He replaces it with “life eternal”, and the phrase comes from Matthew 25:46 — the verse whose first half (“shall go away into everlasting punishment”) he had already taken at 9:16 for the everlasting fire. So the substitution is not a lapse of memory but a splice: the Pauline antithesis is completed out of the Matthean judgment scene the chapter has been quarrying since its middle. Paul's contrast is between two present dispositions and their present fruits; Jacob's is between two eternal destinations, and the changed word is what performs the change.

9:39.note: The clearest quotation in the chapter and one of the clearest in the book: “Remember, to be carnally minded, is death, and to be spiritually minded, is life eternal” against “For to be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life and peace.” Fourteen words in sequence with one substitution, from the KJV's one verse containing “carnally minded”. Still below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold, and not one of his passages. The 1830 prints “carnally minded” and “spiritually minded” open, as the KJV does; 1920 hyphenated both, so the first edition again preserves the source's typography where the modern text obscures it.

9:40.text: Give ear to my words, O LORD, consider my meditation.

provenance.other: “give ear to my words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 5:1.
provenance.significance: Psalm 5:1 is a man asking God to listen — “Give ear to my words, O LORD, consider my meditation” — and Jacob has reversed the direction of the appeal, asking a congregation to listen to him. The reversal is licensed by what he says next: “I have spoken the words of your Maker.” The words the people are asked to give ear to are not his, so the psalm's construction, in which the words given ear to are God's business, survives the change of addressee. The psalm continues “my King, and my God: for unto thee will I pray”, and Jacob's sermon ends at 9:52 telling them to “pray unto him continually”.

9:40.note: A five-word KJV singleton in a verse otherwise made of Jacob's own idiom. The identification is safe on the phrase and the argument is about what the reversal does; graded moderate rather than high because the words are all common in themselves and because an exhortation to hear is the most predictable thing a preacher can say. What is not predictable is that the KJV's one instance of this exact formula is a prayer, and that Jacob's use of it is immediately defended by the claim that the words are God's.

9:41.text: Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.

provenance.other: “narrow is the way” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 7:14; “none other name” occurs in exactly one, Acts 4:12.
provenance.significance: Matthew 7:13-14 gives a gate and a way, and says the gate is strait and the way narrow. Jacob keeps both and adds what Matthew does not have: a keeper. “The keeper of the gate is the Holy One of Israel; and he employeth no servant there.” The addition is a denial — no servant — and it is the sort of denial that answers something. What it answers is not in Matthew; the porter who opens the gate belongs to John 10:3. Whether the denial is aimed there is beyond what the wording will support, but the sentence is constructed as a correction of somebody.

9:41.note: Two elements of Matthew 7:13-14, gate and narrow way, with a philological curiosity between them. The KJV's gate is *strait*, meaning narrow, and its way is *narrow*; the 1830 keeps “narrow” for the way and then writes that it “lieth in a straight course before him”, which is the homophone with its geometric sense. Whether that is a compositor's spelling or the text's own reading, the effect is that the KJV's two words for narrowness have become one word for narrowness and one for directness. The verse closes on Acts 4:12's exclusivity formula — “there is none other way, save it be by the gate” against “there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved” — the KJV's one such construction about salvation, and the chapter's argument at 9:23-24 has just been about a name.

9:42.text: For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it shall be opened.

provenance.other: “knocketh it shall be opened” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 7:8 and Luke 11:10, which are verbally identical at this point.
provenance.significance: Matthew's promise is unconditional — every one that asketh receiveth, and to him that knocketh it shall be opened. Jacob quotes the promise and then withdraws it from a named class: “And whoso knocketh, to him will he open, and the wise, and the learned, and they that are rich … he will not open unto them”, unless they cast these things away. The suppressed context is that Matthew's saying stands six verses before the strait gate Jacob has just used at 9:41; he has taken two consecutive paragraphs of the Sermon on the Mount and set the second against the first, so that the door which opens to all opens to nobody who arrives puffed up.

9:42.note: The Matthew/Luke pair cannot be separated on wording — the two verses are identical where Jacob touches them — so the source is argued from the immediate company: 9:41 has just used Matthew 7:14, which has no Lucan counterpart in that form. That is the same kind of argument made at 9:30 for Matthew 6:21 over Luke 12:34, and it should be weighed once rather than twice. Jacob's construction reverses the KJV's voice, “to him will he open” for “it shall be opened”, which supplies the agent Matthew leaves in the passive — and the agent, per 9:41, is the keeper of the gate who employs no servant.

9:42.text: Let no man deceive himself. If any man among you seemeth to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise.

provenance.other: “let him become a fool” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 3:18. “Puffed up” occurs in six KJV verses, five of them in 1 Corinthians (4:6, 4:18, 4:19, 5:2, 13:4) and one in Colossians — so both of this verse's distinctive terms come from the same letter.
provenance.significance: 1 Corinthians 3:18 is the verse immediately before 3:19, which 2 Nephi 9:28 has already used. Jacob's chapter therefore takes two consecutive verses of 1 Corinthians 3 and separates them by fourteen verses of his own sermon, using the second first: the wisdom that is foolishness at 9:28, the becoming a fool in order to be wise at 9:42. Reading the source's context restores the sequence and shows that the two passages of 2 Nephi 9 that concern learning are one borrowing, split.

9:42.note: “Save they shall cast these things away, and consider themselves fools before God, and come down in the depths of humility, he will not open unto them.” Paul's imperative — if any man seemeth to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise — is here a condition of entry, and Jacob's “puffed up because of their learning” takes the other half of Paul's Corinthian vocabulary for the same fault. The two terms are not a general pair in the KJV; they belong to one letter, and to the four chapters of it that argue about wisdom.

9:43.text: In that hour Jesus rejoiced in spirit, and said, I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes: even so, Father; for so it seemed good in thy sight.

provenance.other: “wise and prudent” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 11:25 and Luke 10:21. tools/mediation-check.py finds no decisive divergence between them at any point 2 Nephi 9:43 reproduces — the two Gospels differ at the frame (“At that time … answered” against “In that hour … rejoiced in spirit”) and not at the saying — so the choice is argued from elsewhere.
provenance.significance: In both Gospels the things hidden from the wise and prudent are revealed unto babes, and the hiding is a matter for thanksgiving. Jacob keeps the hiding, drops the babes, and substitutes what is hidden: not the revelation but “that happiness which is prepared for the Saints”. The consequence is severe in a way neither Gospel is — in Matthew and Luke the wise merely fail to receive; in 2 Nephi 9:43 the happiness prepared for others is withheld from them for ever, which turns a saying about revelation into a sentence about damnation, and lands it in the middle of the passage on learning that runs from 9:28 to 9:43.

9:43.note: Luke is named as the source rather than Matthew on a chapter-level argument: 2 Nephi 9:34's “thrust down to hell” is a Luke 10:15 singleton whose Matthean parallel reads “brought down to hell”, so this chapter demonstrably has Luke 10 in hand, and Luke 10:21 stands six verses from Luke 10:15. The wording itself cannot decide, and Matthew 11:25 is recorded as a composite rather than dismissed. This is the mediation case in the chapter I am least able to close, and it is offered as an argument from company, which is weaker than a word test and should be read as such.

9:44.text: And when they opposed themselves, and blasphemed, he shook his raiment, and said unto them, Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean; from henceforth I will go unto the Gentiles.

provenance.other: “shook his raiment” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 18:6; “pure from the blood” occurs in exactly one, Acts 20:26.
provenance.significance: Acts 18:6 is the whole of Jacob's gesture in one sentence: “he shook his raiment, and said unto them, Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean.” Paul does it at the moment he abandons a synagogue for the Gentiles, and Acts 20:26 repeats the formula at Miletus in his farewell — “I am pure from the blood of all men” — which is the setting Jacob's verse actually occupies, the last address of a preacher who will not have another chance. The metalepsis is the transfer of a missionary's disclaimer to a man addressing his own people in their own temple: Paul shakes his raiment at those who reject him, and Jacob shakes his garments at a congregation he is still trying to save.

9:44.note: Three elements in Acts 18:6's order — the garments shaken, the hearers' blood, the speaker's innocence — recast as a first-person ritual: “I take off my garments, and I shake them before you … that I stand with brightness before him, and am rid of your blood.” Jacob adds an act the KJV does not have, the taking off before the shaking, which converts a gesture of dust-shaking into something closer to Nehemiah 5:13's shaking out of the lap as an oath, and adds the judgment-day frame the source lacks. The link is the chapter's clearest borrowing from Acts, and it is placed where it is because “shook his raiment” is a KJV singleton and no other verse pairs it with blood.

9:45.text: O come, let us sing unto the LORD: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation.

provenance.other: “rock of our salvation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 95:1; “the rock of my salvation” occurs in exactly two, 2 Samuel 22:47 and Psalm 89:26; Deuteronomy 32:15 has “the Rock of his salvation”. The Book of Mormon's “the rock of your salvation” is the one person of the formula the KJV never uses.
provenance.significance: Every KJV form of the phrase is spoken by the worshipper about his own God — our rock, my rock, or, in Deuteronomy 32:15, Jeshurun's rock forsaken. Jacob turns it to the second person and hands it to his hearers: “come unto that God which is the rock of your salvation.” The nearest source, Psalm 95:1, opens the psalm whose second half is the wilderness warning (“harden not your heart, as in the provocation”) that Hebrews 3-4 makes the type of apostasy — which is what Jacob's verse is about, men bound by chains who must turn away from their sins.

9:45.note: The paradigm is filled out in a person no KJV verse uses, which is evidence of a formula being handled rather than a verse being copied. Psalm 95:1 is named as the source because it is the closest form and because its psalm is the one about hardening the heart, but Deuteronomy 32:15 has a claim too: Jeshurun waxes fat and forsakes the Rock of his salvation, and Jacob's next breath at 9:51 is “let your soul delight in fatness”, the same figure turned to good. Graded moderate on the person shift and the plurality of candidates.
9:45.whyNot: Four words, one of them a possessive that matches nothing in the KJV, and the rock-of-salvation figure is spread across Deuteronomy, 2 Samuel and the Psalms. No single verse can be pinned.

9:46.text: And I heard another out of the altar say, Even so, Lord God Almighty, true and righteous are thy judgments.

provenance.route: Revelation 16:7 and 4:8 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “true and righteous are thy judgments” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 16:7; “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty” occurs in exactly one, Revelation 4:8.
provenance.significance: Jacob's damned man cries “Holy, holy are thy judgments, O Lord God Almighty”, which is not a KJV sentence but is exactly two KJV sentences fused. Revelation 16:7 supplies the frame — an acclamation of God's judgments addressed to the Lord God Almighty, spoken out of the altar as the vials are poured out — and Revelation 4:8 supplies the substituted predicate, the trisagion of the four beasts. The fusion is doctrinally loaded: the vindication of God's justice in Revelation 16 is sung by the altar, and in 2 Nephi 9:46 it is put in the mouth of the man being judged, who goes on to say “I know my guilt; I transgressed thy law”. Note that Revelation 15:3-4 is the immediate context of both, and 1 Nephi 1:14 already borrowed six words from Revelation 15:3.

9:46.note: Two Revelation verses spliced at the point where they share “Lord God Almighty”. Jacob has the shorter double “Holy, holy” rather than the trisagion — the third repetition is dropped, as it is nowhere else in the KJV — and has moved the adjective from God to God's judgments, where Revelation 16:7 has “true and righteous”. The result says something neither source says: that the judgments themselves are holy, conceded by the man they fall on. This is the third distinct borrowing from Revelation in the chapter (20:13 at 9:12, 14:11 and 20:10 at 9:16), and the fourth if the paradise of God at 9:13 holds.

9:50.text: Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.

provenance.other: “he that hath no money” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 55:1. The machine stream scored a sixteen-word contiguous run here, the longest in the chapter by a wide margin.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 55 opens the last movement of Second Isaiah, immediately after the barren woman's song of Isaiah 54 — and Jacob has been expounding Isaiah 49-52 since 2 Nephi 6, with Isaiah 50 and 51:1-52:2 transcribed in the two chapters that follow this one. So the invitation he ends his day's preaching with is the passage that stands just past the block he is working through: he closes with the text his exposition is heading toward. The suppressed context is Isaiah 55:3, “I will make an everlasting covenant with you, even the sure mercies of David”, which is the covenant language 9:1 opened the sermon with.

9:50.note: Sixteen consecutive words of Isaiah 55:1 with one substitution and one deletion: the KJV's “Ho, every one that thirsteth” becomes “Come, my brethren, every one that thirsteth”, replacing the prophetic hail with a preacher's address, and the second “come ye” before “buy” is dropped. This is at Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is one of the few passages in the chapter that would meet it, but it is not among his thirty-six and no claim is made that it is. The verse is quoted, not transcribed — it sits inside Jacob's own sermon and is introduced by his own vocative — which is why it is adjudicated by hand rather than collated with tools/collate-isaiah.py.

9:51.text: Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness.

provenance.other: “let your soul delight itself in fatness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 55:2.
provenance.significance: Isaiah's question — why spend money for that which is not bread? — is rhetorical, and Jacob converts it into a command: “do not spend money for that which is of no worth.” The change of mood is the whole of his exposition. Isaiah asks the exiles why they do a foolish thing; Jacob forbids a congregation to do it, and then replaces Isaiah's “eat ye that which is good” with “feast upon that which perisheth not, neither can be corrupted”, which imports the chapter's own resurrection vocabulary (9:7's incorruption, 9:13's incorruptible) into the prophet's meal. The Isaiah invitation has been made an invitation to the incorruptible body.

9:51.note: Isaiah 55:2 in sequence with three departures, each of which does work. The interrogative becomes an imperative; “that which is not bread” becomes “that which is of no worth” and “satisfieth not” becomes “cannot satisfy”, both flattening a concrete figure into a valuation; and the reflexive drops out of the final clause, so that the KJV's “let your soul delight itself in fatness” becomes “let your soul delight in fatness”. The 1830 has the shorter form, so this is not a later modernisation. Between the two departures Jacob inserts a sentence of his own — “remember the words which I have spoken; and come unto the Holy One of Israel” — which is how the chapter has handled every long borrowing: the source is carried, and Jacob's own title for God is set inside it.

9:53.text: Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth.

provenance.other: “righteous Branch” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jeremiah 23:5; Jeremiah 33:15 has “the Branch of righteousness”.
provenance.significance: In Jeremiah the righteous Branch is a single messianic king raised unto David, and in 2 Nephi 9:53 it is a surviving remnant: “our seed shall not utterly be destroyed … in future generations, they shall become a righteous branch unto the House of Israel.” The figure has been transposed from one person to a people, which is the same transposition the Book of Mormon's whole covenant argument depends on — the Lehite seed as the branch broken off and preserved. Jacob's sermon opened at 9:1 on the covenants with all the house of Israel; it closes with the house of Israel receiving a branch back.

9:53.note: A KJV singleton in an unexpected sense. Jeremiah's Branch is Davidic and royal; Jacob's is genealogical, a preserved seed rather than a coming king, and “unto the House of Israel” takes the place of Jeremiah's “unto David”. Graded moderate because two words are all that is shared and “branch” is common in the KJV; what makes the row worth having is that the one verse pairing branch with righteous is a promise of preservation to a people about to be scattered, which is exactly what Jacob is promising.
